name: Switching Costs

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether existing customers face real value loss from switching and whether repeat economics let the company capture a durable Benefit.
positioning.productLabel: Switching Costs Lens — based on Hamilton Helmer's public 7 Powers materials
notAClaimOf: customer harm or artificial obstruction being a desirable product strategy

attribution.display: Based on Hamilton Helmer's public Switching Costs doctrine

neutralParaphrase: Switching Costs may exist when an existing customer expects material operational, financial, procedural, relational, data, integration, training, or risk loss from changing suppliers. The company can capture a Benefit only when follow-on purchases or repeat economic interactions exist. Retention alone is ambiguous, and acquisition competition, portability, contract expiry, customer resentment, or new architecture can erode the advantage.

Abstract: heterogeneous consumers, imperfect lock-in, and non-monotonic price effects

requiredConditions: The customer makes repeat purchases or has recurring economic interaction.
Switching loss is measured from the customer's perspective.
Retention causes are separated from satisfaction, contract, inertia, and lack of alternatives.
The company can capture value without destroying the customer relationship.

requiredEvidence.description: Customer-level migration cost, downtime, data loss, retraining, integration work, operational risk, relationship rebuilding, and foregone value.
Renewal, follow-on product, usage, expansion, maintenance, or repeat-purchase economics through which the company may capture Benefit.
Evidence separating true switching loss from customer satisfaction, product superiority, price, contract duration, and missing alternatives.
Data portability, interoperability, migration tools, regulation, new architecture, competitor incentives, and CAC needed to dislodge or acquire customers.

decisionQuestions: What value would an existing customer lose by switching today?
Which losses are unavoidable and which are intentionally imposed?
What repeat interaction lets the company capture the Benefit?
How much must a competitor compensate or assist the customer to switch?
Could portability, AI migration, standards, or regulation sharply reduce the Barrier?
Does pricing behavior preserve trust or create an opening for displacement?
positiveSignals: Completed migration projects show material cost, time, risk, or workflow disruption.
Customer cohorts demonstrate repeat economics beyond contract duration.
Competitors must fund meaningful migration assistance or price concessions.
Switching loss rises through legitimate accumulated value, not artificial obstruction.
Portability and interoperability stress tests leave a material residual Barrier.
redFlags: Retention or net revenue retention is the only evidence.
Multi-year contracts are treated as permanent switching cost.
The customer has no follow-on purchase or recurring interaction.
High churn appears immediately at renewal or contract expiry.
New migration tools, open standards, or regulation can remove the loss.
disconfirmingEvidence: Customers switch with little downtime, cost, or value loss.
A competitor routinely pays migration cost and still earns attractive economics.
Retention is explained by current product superiority rather than lock-in.
Customer acquisition competition eliminates the lifetime-value Benefit.
Artificial friction produces backlash, regulation, or rapid substitute adoption.
contraindications: Do not infer Switching Costs from retention alone.
Do not celebrate harmful or deceptive lock-in.
Do not assume pricing power follows mechanically from customer loss.
Do not count the same embedding again as Process or Network Power without causal separation.

instructions: Map switching losses for representative customer cohorts.
Identify the repeat interaction and possible company Benefit.
Stress competitor compensation, migration technology, regulation, and trust.
Conclude on observed, candidate, path, unsupported, or inapplicable Switching Costs.

sourceReliability.low: Only retention metrics or founder claims are available.
sourceReliability.medium: Customer interviews, contracts, and cohort data are available.
sourceReliability.high: Observed migration evidence, causal retention analysis, and competitor offers converge.

evidenceStrength.medium: Loss is material but capture or persistence is uncertain.
evidenceStrength.high: Customer loss, repeat Benefit, competitor disadvantage, and persistence are supported.

evidenceCoverage.low: Migration loss or repeat economics are missing.
evidenceCoverage.medium: Core loss and retention are covered but portability or CAC is incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: Loss, repeat interaction, causal retention, portability, competition, trust, and decay are covered.

applicabilityConfidence.low: The product is transactional or easily replaced.
applicabilityConfidence.medium: Some customer workflow or data accumulates.
applicabilityConfidence.high: The product is deeply embedded in recurring customer operations.

judgmentConfidence.medium: Candidate switching loss exists with unresolved economic capture.
judgmentConfidence.high: Observed customer loss and durable repeat Benefit are supported.

promotionRequirements: Complete licensed Switching Costs chapter review.
Validate migration-loss and causal-retention fields by business model.
Test whether the lens adds value beyond retention, contract length, and NRR.
empiricalQualifications: Switching-cost effects on equilibrium price and competition are model-dependent.
Portability, migration automation, standards, regulation, and customer backlash can shorten duration.

rights.notes: Public interview doctrine and external research are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Verify direct audio locators and precise follow-on-purchase condition.
